paras: The killing and cremation of Albert Washington was the shooting of a Black man by two police sergeants near Shreveport, Louisiana, on April 11, 1903, and the burning of his body by a mob early the next morning, after he was suspected in the ax murder of Mrs. Alice Matthews. First reported as Ed Porter, he was shot in the back as he ran, and about 100 men later burned his body on a pyre. Within days a coroner's jury attributed the murder to a person unknown, his employers placed him miles away, and papers in both presses reported that an innocent man had been killed.

Mrs. Matthews, wife of civil engineer Frank Matthews, was found dead in her bed early on Saturday, April 11, and her ten-year-old daughter Aline was found badly wounded. The first dispatches said she had been "criminally assaulted" with a bloody ax found in the kitchen. After bloodhounds lost the trail, a railroad engineer reported a Black man covered with blood on the Kansas City Southern tracks, and a posse was organized to hunt him.

According to the Shreveport dispatch, Sergeants Gerald and Roquemore came upon the man about five miles from the city and, when he ran for a ravine, fired four shots, two of which struck him in the back and killed him. The dispatch said his clothing was bloody and his shoes fitted footprints in the Matthews kitchen. The Caucasian, a Shreveport paper, said he ran when officers halted him in a railroad cut and asked about blood on his person.

The sheriff, the mayor and the chief of police had the body moved beyond the crowd's reach. At about 1:30 a.m. on Sunday, April 12, a mob of about 100 men took it from the cemetery and burned it on a pyre, at the head of Texas Street by one account and on the levee by another.

On Sunday afternoon a coroner's jury under Dr. Coty found that Mrs. Matthews had died "from wounds inflicted by a person unknown to them" and urged a grand jury investigation. On the word of Bossier planters Cal Vance and Mr. Stinson, The Caucasian identified the dead man as Albert Washington, a hand who had been on their plantation until he took the 10 o'clock train to Shreveport that morning. It added that his coat belonged to an Ed Porter of Bossier, that a juror found the Ed Porter named by an officer "alive and well," and that the blood came from handling beef and from his wounds.

Officials still insisted the right man had been killed, while Mrs. Phillips, a boarder behind the Matthews house, told of seeing a man leave its back door and run down the alley. No report of a grand jury finding or of action against the officers or the mob was found. In July the Courier-Journal reported that Mrs. Matthews' son suspected Jennie Steer, a Black servant in the house who had been lynched in another case.

The first wire ran from April 12 in papers from Louisville to New York and Arizona under headlines such as "FIENDISH," presenting the dead man as the killer. A Portland dispatch claimed a bloody ring of the victim was in his clothes, which The Caucasian denied. The Caucasian called the burning "a mistake" but held the officers "justified in law and reason to shoot," and the Brandon News answered the Meridian Press's charge of murder with "This was not murder." Other white papers, from Hattiesburg to Salt Lake City and River Falls, said a mob had "lynched the wrong negro."

Shreveport's two Black papers, quoted by The Caucasian, denied rumors of retaliation; the News-Enterprise said "a mistake has been made," and the Watchman urged readers to "keep cool." Northern Black papers were sharper: the Detroit Plaindealer saw Black men killed "to hide some white man's crime" and urged armed self-defense, and the Cleveland Gazette said he was "brutally lynched."

Accounts differ on his name, given as Ed Porter, Albert Washington or Ed Washington, and on the blood, explained as beef, a goose or his own wounds; the Caucasian's identification, resting on named employers and a juror's inquiry, is the most detailed.

reader.title: Killing and cremation of Albert Washington
bases: A man suspected of a murder was shot dead by two police sergeants from a posse organized to hunt him, and his body was then taken and burned by a mob of about 100 (A2, A3, A18).

He was hunted by an organized posse and shot while fleeing by two of its members, police sergeants, whom the local paper called legally justified, while the Meridian Press called it murder (A2, A19, A36); a mob of about 100 then took and burned the body (A3, A18). Contemporaries in both presses called the episode a lynching (A21, A26, A39, A44), but the killing itself was done by two officers claiming arrest authority, so legality and group size are unclear.

The shooting by two police sergeants and the mob burning of the body are reported independently by the Shreveport wire, the local Caucasian and Louisiana and Black papers (A2, A3, A18, A33, A38), though his identity and guilt are disputed.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire (officers' account)
accounts.gist: A Black man covered with blood fled toward a ravine when two sergeants came upon him and was shot dead; his shoes fitted bloody footprints in the Matthews kitchen.

accounts.label: Planters and plantation hands
accounts.gist: Cal Vance and Mr. Stinson said the dead man was Albert Washington, who was in Bossier until the 10 a.m. train Saturday; hands from the plantation identified the body.

accounts.label: The Caucasian (local editor)
accounts.gist: An innocent man was probably killed and the cremation was a mistake, but the officers were justified in shooting a fleeing man.

accounts.label: Mrs. Phillips
accounts.gist: She saw a man, a white man in later versions, leave the back of the Matthews house about the time of the murder and run down the alley.

accounts.label: Black correspondents
accounts.gist: The man was innocent, killed to cover a white man's crime; the Plaindealer says police shot him, the Cleveland Gazette says he was lynched by a mob.

accounts.label: Son's later account
accounts.gist: Porter Matthews came to believe his mother was killed by a woman for $30 and not assaulted, and suspicion fell on the servant Jennie Steer.

framing.detail: The first wire ran under headlines such as 'FIENDISH' and 'NEGRO MURDERER SHOT,' treating the dead man as the rapist-murderer.
The Shreveport Caucasian called the burning 'a mistake' and doubted his guilt but held the officers 'justified in law and reason to shoot.'
The Brandon News headed its answer to the Meridian Press 'NOT MURDER' and blamed 'transient negroes'; the Hattiesburg Progress first wrote of 'the brute nature of the negro.'
Hattiesburg's 'LYNCHED THE WRONG MAN,' the Salt Lake Herald and the River Falls Journal treated it as a mob lynching of an innocent man.
The Plaindealer called it 'killing poor, defenseless Negroes to hide some white man's crime'; the Cleveland Gazette headlined 'Another Innocent Afro-American Murdered by Burly White Brutes.'
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate asked how many more must suffer 'before lynch law is a thing of the past even in Louisiana.'
